 Regional perspectives on air quality and health: WHO Western Pacific Region: technical brief
 Science and policy snapshots on air quality, energy and health
 18 November 2026 
  |  Technical document 
 Download (2.1 MB) 
 Overview 
 This technical brief examines air pollution and its health impacts in the WHO Western Pacific Region, where exposure contributes to more than 2 million deaths annually, predominantly from noncommunicable diseases. Major pollution sources include fossil fuel combustion, transport, industrial activities, agricultural burning and household use of polluting fuels and technologies. Despite progress in establishing national air quality standards, substantial gaps remain between regulatory limits and WHO recommendations, while monitoring capacity varies considerably across countries. 
 The brief reviews regional evidence, policy responses and challenges in reducing air pollution, highlighting opportunities to integrate air quality management with climate change mitigation and public health objectives. Experiences from Australia, China, the Philippines and the Republic of Korea illustrate national and municipal interventions. Priority actions include strengthening air quality standards and monitoring, expanding access to clean household energy, promoting multisectoral and transboundary cooperation, building health workforce capacity and mobilizing financing to accelerate pollution reduction and protect population health.
 This document is part of the WHO Air Quality, Energy, and Health Science and Policy Summaries (SPS). These summaries provide concise overviews of current knowledge and evidence on air quality, energy access, climate change, and health. They aim to support decision-makers by presenting key insights from scientific research.
 The SPS are developed through a multistakeholder consultation process that includes experts from WHO Advisory Groups – i.e., the Scientific Advisory Group on Air Pollution and Health (SAG) , and the Global Air Pollution and Health – Technical Advisory Group (GAPH-TAG) – as well as specialists from WHO Collaborating Centres , UN agencies as well as other experts from academia and civil society.
